case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
case.limits: The court read the statute's word individual and expressly left open how much AI assistance a human inventor may use. The unsettled question is inventorship quality, not machine inventorship, which is closed.
case.holding: An inventor under the Patent Act must be a natural person, so a patent application naming an AI system as the sole inventor is properly refused without reaching whether the system actually conceived anything.

live_cases.name: University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC

case.why_ai_cites_it: The controlling answer to AI-invented subject matter: whatever a system devises, the application must name a human inventor. Companies cite it when structuring filings around human contributors; challengers cite it to attack patents where the human contribution looks nominal.

reading.body:
The Federal Circuit's 2022 ruling in *Thaler v. Vidal* closes one question completely: a patent application that names only an AI system as inventor will be refused, because the Patent Act's word "individual" requires a natural person.

The court did not need to decide whether the AI system actually conceived the invention, and it did not. That procedural economy matters. The holding rests on statutory interpretation alone, which means the underlying question of whether machine conception can qualify as conception at all remains untouched by this case. What the ruling does settle, practically, is filing structure: any application must carry at least one human name in the inventor line.

The limit the court expressly left open is how much AI assistance a human inventor may use and still satisfy the inventorship requirement. That gap is now the live frontier. A company whose engineers used AI heavily during conception faces a different legal question than the one *Thaler* answered, and the outcome of that question is not yet determined. The one linked live case in this dataset, *UTRF v. Anthropic*, signals that inventorship doctrine continues to generate active litigation, though this data covers only that single pending matter and does not describe its facts or posture in detail.
